title: Australia | APRA CPS 234 Information Security, CPS 230 Resilience and the Privacy Act
tagline: Protect bank data and services the Australian way: CPS 234 security, CPS 230 resilience, APP 11 and the data breach scheme.
sectors: Bank technology, security and operations teams
Bank risk, compliance, privacy and internal audit functions
description:
This quest teaches Australian bank staff how information security, operational resilience and privacy fit together under three sources: APRA's **Prudential Standard CPS 234 Information Security** and its practice guide **CPG 234**, APRA's **Prudential Standard CPS 230 Operational Risk Management** (in force since 1 July 2025), and the **Privacy Act 1988**, including **APP 11** and the **Notifiable Data Breaches** scheme in Part IIIC, regulated by the **OAIC**.

CPS 234 requires banks to keep an information security capability that matches their threats and makes the board ultimately responsible. APRA's guidance describes an awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tested at commencement and periodically. This quest serves that need for all bank staff, with deeper material for managers, risk teams and directors.

Across five stages you follow a fictional team at Wattle Coast Bank through the board's duties, controls and testing, APRA notifications, phishing and social engineering, data breach decisions, critical operations, tolerance levels and service providers.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or advice from your security, privacy and compliance teams.
audience: All staff and contractors at Australian banks who use the bank's systems or handle customer information
Contact centre, branch and operations staff who are targets of phishing and social engineering
Technology, security and operations teams who run controls, testing and incident response
Risk, privacy, compliance and internal audit staff who oversee CPS 234, CPS 230 and Privacy Act duties
Senior managers and directors accountable for information security and operational resilience
outcomes: Explain CPS 234's requirements and the board's ultimate responsibility for information security
Apply CPS 234's rules on controls, testing, response plans and the 72-hour and 10-business-day APRA notices
Recognise and report phishing, vishing, tailgating and other social engineering in line with CPG 234 good practice
Apply APP 11 and decide whether an incident is an eligible data breach under the Privacy Act
Describe CPS 230 critical operations, tolerance levels, BCP testing and material service provider duties
Summarise the evidence a bank needs to show APRA and auditors that its program works

quest.name: Wattle Coast Shield
quest.premise: You have just joined the Information Security Office at Wattle Coast Bank in Brisbane. With CISO Mei Lin Zhao, operational risk manager Callum Reid, privacy officer Amara Mensah, Perth contact centre leader Raj Menon and board risk chair Sofia Marchetti, you must turn APRA's standards and the Privacy Act into decisions in the boardroom, the security operations centre and the phone queue.

badge.name: Wattle Coast Shield Bearer
badge.description: Awarded for demonstrating working knowledge of APRA CPS 234, CPS 230 and the Privacy Act's security and data breach duties for Australian banks.

sessions.title: CPS 234 foundations: board, roles, capability and classification
sessions.summary: Meet APRA's CPS 234 Information Security: its aim, the board's ultimate responsibility, defined roles, a capability that matches the threats, the policy framework, asset classification and third-party assets.
objectives: Explain the purpose and scope of CPS 234 for authorised deposit-taking institutions
Describe the board's ultimate responsibility and the roles CPS 234 requires to be defined
Classify information assets by criticality and sensitivity
Apply CPS 234 to assets managed by related parties and third parties

cards.title: Stage one: the security charter
cards.setting: Board room, Wattle Coast Bank head office, Brisbane. Monday, 8:40 am.

lines.text: Your new lanyard reads 'Information Security Office'. Through the glass you can see a whiteboard covered in four letters: CPS 234.
Welcome aboard. I'm Mei Lin Zhao, the bank's chief information security officer. You're joining the team that keeps our customers' data and money safe.
Sofia Marchetti, I chair the board risk committee. I'll be blunt: under APRA's standard the board is ultimately responsible for information security. Not IT. Us.
Callum Reid, operational risk. And since July 2025 we also live under CPS 230, so security and resilience now sit side by side in my world.
Amara Mensah, privacy officer. When something goes wrong with customer data, the Privacy Act and the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme land on my desk.
(video call from the Perth contact centre) Raj Menon, team leader. My people get fake 'IT support' calls every week. I need something they can actually use.
So that's your mission: five stages, from the boardroom to the phone queue. First stop, what CPS 234 actually asks of a bank. Ready?

scenes.heading: Who sets the rule
scenes.narration: APRA, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, supervises banks and other deposit-takers. It made Prudential Standard CPS 234 Information Security, which has applied since 1 July 2019.

scenes.heading: The aim
scenes.narration: The standard wants each regulated entity to be resilient against information security incidents, including cyber-attacks, by keeping a security capability that matches the threats it faces.

scenes.heading: Three properties
scenes.narration: Information security means preserving three things: confidentiality, so only authorised people get access; integrity, so data stays complete and accurate; and availability, so systems work when needed.

scenes.heading: The board on the hook
scenes.narration: The board is ultimately responsible for the entity's information security. It must make sure security keeps pace with the size of the threats and supports the bank's sound operation.

scenes.heading: Beyond our walls
scenes.narration: The duties reach information assets that related parties and third parties manage for the bank. Outsourcing a system does not outsource the responsibility.

cards.title: Who owns information security
cards.caption: CPS 234 requires the entity to define the security roles of the board, senior management, governing bodies and individuals.

items.label: Board
items.detail: Ultimately responsible; sets direction and oversees whether security matches the threats.

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Roles defined in writing; runs the capability and reports to the board.

items.label: Committees and forums
items.detail: Governing bodies with decision, approval or oversight roles named clearly.

items.label: Security specialists
items.detail: Operate controls, testing, monitoring and incident response.

items.label: Every staff member and contractor
items.detail: Follows the policy framework and reports concerns quickly.

cards.question: Under CPS 234, who is ultimately responsible for a bank's information security?
options: The chief information security officer
The board of the bank
APRA's supervision team
The bank's main technology vendor
cards.explanation: The standard places ultimate responsibility on the board. The CISO and others carry defined roles, but they act under the board's oversight; a vendor never takes over the bank's responsibility.

cards.title: Criticality versus sensitivity
cards.caption: CPS 234 requires every information asset, including those held by third parties, to be classified by both.

items.label: Question it answers
items.right: What if confidentiality or integrity is lost?

items.label: Typical example
items.right: Customer identity files leak or are altered

items.label: Who is harmed
items.left: Customers who cannot pay or access funds
items.right: Customers exposed to fraud or identity theft

cards.title: What CPS 234 requires, in plain words
cards.body:
CPS 234 is short, but each paragraph carries weight. A bank must:

- **Define roles**: write down the security responsibilities of the board, senior management, committees and individuals.
- **Keep a capability** (people, skills, resources and controls) that matches the size and extent of the threats, and keep it current as threats and systems change.
- **Maintain a policy framework** that tells *everyone* with a security duty what to do: staff, contractors, consultants, related parties, third parties and even customers.
- **Classify information assets** by criticality and sensitivity, including assets managed by others.
- **Implement controls** in a timely way, sized to threats, asset value, life-cycle stage and the consequences of an incident.
- **Detect, respond, test and audit**, and **notify APRA** of material incidents and control weaknesses.

The key idea is *commensurate*: the stronger the threat and the more valuable the asset, the stronger the protection must be.

cards.title: Match the CPS 234 term
cards.prompt: Link each term from the standard to its meaning, in your own words.

pairs.right: Information and IT, including software, hardware and data, in soft or hard copy
An actual or potential compromise of information security
A weakness in an asset or control that could be exploited
A circumstance or event that could exploit a weakness
A prevention, detection or response measure that lowers likelihood or impact
All the resources, skills and controls that let the bank maintain security

lines.text: Procurement wants to sign a new cloud provider for our loan document archive this week. They say the provider is 'ISO-certified, so we're covered'.
A certificate is a starting point. CPS 234 says we must assess the provider's security capability and evaluate the design of the controls protecting our data.
Even though the provider runs the systems?
Especially then. The archive holds identity documents for thousands of borrowers. Its sensitivity is high, so our checks need to be deep.
And if it goes wrong, the board can't tell APRA it was the vendor's problem. What's the right call here?

cards.title: Signing the cloud archive deal
cards.situation: Procurement wants to sign a cloud provider for the loan document archive by Friday. The provider offers an ISO 27001 certificate and a standard contract. Nobody in the security team has reviewed the controls that would protect the bank's documents, and the business is pushing hard for the deadline.

choices.text: Sign now on the strength of the certificate and review the controls after go-live.
choices.outcome: The bank would be relying on a certificate whose scope may not even cover the archive service. CPS 234 expects the bank to assess the provider's capability and evaluate control design before trusting it with sensitive assets.

choices.text: Pause signing until security assesses the provider's capability, the scope of its certification and the design of the controls for our data, sized to the archive's sensitivity.
choices.outcome: This matches CPS 234: third-party capability is assessed in proportion to the consequences of an incident, and the design of the provider's controls over the bank's assets is evaluated. The deadline moves a little; the risk falls a lot.

choices.text: Sign, but add a clause making the provider liable for any breach.
choices.outcome: A liability clause helps with money, not with security. The bank would still not know whether the controls are adequate, and responsibility to APRA stays with the bank.

cards.front: Myth: information security is an IT matter.
cards.back: Fact: CPS 234 makes the board ultimately responsible and requires roles for senior management, committees and individuals.

cards.front: Myth: if a vendor runs the system, its security is the vendor's problem.
cards.back: Fact: the bank must assess third-party capability, evaluate control design and include those assets in testing and audit.

cards.front: Myth: paper files are outside CPS 234.
cards.back: Fact: information assets include data in both soft and hard copy.

cards.front: Myth: controls are set once at go-live.
cards.back: Fact: the capability must be actively maintained as threats, assets and the business change.
Fact: it covers any actual or potential compromise of confidentiality, integrity or availability, whatever the cause.

cards.question: A bank classifies its customer identity document store. Which pair of questions does CPS 234 require it to consider?
options: Cost of the system and age of the hardware
Criticality (impact of losing availability) and sensitivity (impact of losing confidentiality or integrity)
Number of users and the vendor's market share
cards.explanation: Classification must be by criticality and sensitivity, reflecting how an incident could affect the bank or its customers financially or otherwise. Cost and vendor size may matter commercially but are not the classification test.

cards.title: Real case: APRA's response to the Medibank cyber incident
cards.body:
In October 2022, health insurer **Medibank** suffered a cyber incident that APRA later called one of the most significant data breaches Australia had experienced. Medibank is APRA-regulated, so CPS 234 applied.

In **June 2023** APRA announced it would increase Medibank's capital adequacy requirement by **AUD 250 million**, effective 1 July 2023, reflecting weaknesses it found in Medibank's information security environment. The adjustment stays until an agreed remediation program is completed to APRA's satisfaction, and APRA said it would run a targeted technology review focused on **governance and risk culture**.

APRA also said it expected appropriate accountability and consequence management, including effects on executive pay where appropriate, and noted that it kept finding poor practices and **inadequate oversight from boards and management** across the industry.

**Lesson for a bank:** weak security is a prudential issue, not just an IT one. APRA can turn control weaknesses into capital costs and close scrutiny of the board.

cards.title: Real case: ASIC v RI Advice (2022)
cards.body:
In **May 2022** the Federal Court found, in an Australian first, that financial services licensee **RI Advice** had breached its licence obligations because it lacked adequate risk management systems for cybersecurity risk. ASIC brought the case.

Between 2014 and 2020 a series of cyber incidents hit practices of RI Advice's authorised representatives. In one, an attacker used a **brute force attack** to reach a representative's file server and stayed undetected for months, potentially exposing personal information of several thousand people.

The court ordered RI Advice to hire a cybersecurity expert to identify and implement any further measures needed across its network, and to pay **AUD 750,000** towards ASIC's costs. The judge observed that cyber risk cannot be cut to zero but can be materially reduced to an acceptable level with adequate documentation and controls.

**Lesson:** for a bank, CPS 234 sets APRA's expectations; ASIC's licensing duties can add a second line of legal exposure when cyber risk is poorly managed.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: CPS 234 has applied to banks and other APRA-regulated entities since 1 July 2019.
The board is ultimately responsible for information security; roles for everyone else must be clearly defined.
Capability, policies and controls must be commensurate with the threats and the value of the assets.
Assets are classified by criticality (availability) and sensitivity (confidentiality and integrity).
Third-party and related-party assets stay inside the bank's responsibility.

cards.prompt: Think of one system you use every day at work. How would you rate its criticality and its sensitivity, and who in your organisation is responsible for its security?

quiz.question: Since when has APRA's CPS 234 Information Security applied to authorised deposit-taking institutions?
options: 1 July 2019
1 July 2015
1 July 2025
1 January 2023
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 commenced on 1 July 2019. 1 July 2025 is the start date of CPS 230 Operational Risk Management, a different standard.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures the main objective of CPS 234?
options: To require every bank to buy security software from approved vendors
To make entities resilient to security incidents by keeping a capability that matches their threats
To make APRA responsible for detecting cyber-attacks on banks
To replace the Privacy Act's security duties for every bank and insurer that APRA regulates in Australia
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 aims for resilience through a security capability commensurate with vulnerabilities and threats. APRA does not run banks' detection, and the Privacy Act still applies alongside it.

quiz.question: A director says: 'Cyber security is the CISO's job; the board only hears about it if something breaks.' How does this fit CPS 234?
options: It fits, provided the CISO reports to the chief executive
It fits, because CPS 234 places responsibility on senior management and leaves the board to receive incident reports
It does not fit: the board is ultimately responsible and must ensure security matches the threats
It does not fit, because APRA requires a director to act as CISO
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 makes the board ultimately responsible for information security. It does not require a director to be the CISO, but it does require active oversight rather than waiting for failures.

quiz.question: A bank's mortgage files are stored in paper form in an offsite facility run by a storage company. Are they inside CPS 234?
options: Yes: information assets include hard copy data, including assets managed by third parties
No: CPS 234 only applies to digital systems
Only if the storage company is itself APRA-regulated, because the standard follows the provider's own licence
Only once the files are scanned into a bank system
quiz.explanation: The definition of information asset covers data in soft and hard copy, and the standard expressly reaches assets managed by related parties and third parties.

quiz.question: In CPS 234 terms, a payments switch that customers rely on every minute but that stores little personal data is most likely to be rated as:
options: High sensitivity, low criticality
Out of scope, because it holds little personal data
Low risk, because availability is not a security property
High criticality, with sensitivity assessed separately
quiz.explanation: Criticality is about the impact of losing availability, so a payments switch rates high. Availability is one of the three security properties, and sensitivity is a separate rating.

quiz.question: Who must the bank's information security policy framework give direction to?
options: Only the information security team
Only employees on permanent contracts, since contractors follow their own employer's rules
All parties with a security obligation, including staff, contractors, third parties and customers
Only the board and senior management
quiz.explanation: The framework must direct everyone with a duty to maintain security. The standard's notes list staff, contractors, consultants, related parties, third parties and customers.

quiz.question: A bank plans to move its customer document archive to a cloud provider. What does CPS 234 require before relying on it?
options: Obtain APRA's written approval of the provider and of the contract before any customer data is moved
Assess the provider's capability and evaluate the design of controls protecting the bank's assets
Nothing, if the provider is certified to an international standard
Ask the provider to sign the bank's staff code of conduct
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 requires the bank to assess third-party capability in line with the consequences of an incident and to evaluate the design of the third party's controls. Certification helps but does not replace that assessment.

quiz.question: What did APRA announce in June 2023 in response to the Medibank cyber incident?
options: A capital adequacy increase of AUD 250 million until agreed remediation was completed
The cancellation of Medibank's registration as a private health insurer until a new board was appointed
A criminal referral of Medibank's directors
A fine of AUD 250 million paid to the Commonwealth
quiz.explanation: APRA applied a capital adjustment of AUD 250 million from 1 July 2023 and announced a targeted technology review. It was a capital measure, not a fine or a licence cancellation.

quiz.question: Which word best summarises how CPS 234 expects controls and capability to be sized?
options: Uniform
Maximal
Optional
Commensurate
quiz.explanation: The standard repeatedly asks for capability, policies, controls and testing commensurate with threats, criticality, sensitivity and consequences. It does not prescribe one uniform level for every asset.

quiz.question: In ASIC v RI Advice (2022), what did the Federal Court find?
options: The licensee breached its obligations by lacking adequate cybersecurity risk management
The licensee was not responsible for incidents at its authorised representatives' separately owned practices
APRA should have supervised the licensee's cyber controls
The licensee had to pay compensation to every affected client
quiz.explanation: The court found RI Advice breached its licence obligations because its cyber risk management systems were inadequate, and ordered it to engage a cybersecurity expert and pay AUD 750,000 towards ASIC's costs.

sessions.title: Controls, testing, incident response and APRA notification
sessions.summary: Turn CPS 234 into practice: commensurate controls, detection, response plans tested every year, independent control testing, internal audit, and the 72-hour and 10-business-day notices to APRA.
objectives: Describe how CPS 234 expects controls to be sized and implemented
Explain the requirements for response plans, control testing and internal audit
Apply the 72-hour incident and 10-business-day weakness notification rules
Escalate a suspected incident correctly from the front line

cards.title: Stage two: the watchtower
cards.setting: Security operations centre, Wattle Coast Bank, Melbourne. Wednesday, 2:05 am.

lines.text: A red tile flashes on the wall screen: unusual data transfer from a server in the home loans environment to an unknown address overseas.
(on the phone, half awake) How much data, and since when?
About 40 gigabytes over three hours. We've blocked the address. We don't yet know what was in it.
Then the clock may already be running. Under CPS 234 we tell APRA within 72 hours of becoming aware of a material incident, and we can't wait for perfect facts.
If customer data left the building, I have Privacy Act duties too. Please loop me in now, not on Friday.
Agreed. Let's run the response plan the way we tested it in March. This is what the drills were for.

scenes.heading: Controls that fit
scenes.narration: CPS 234 requires controls for every information asset, put in place in a timely way and sized to the threats, the asset's criticality and sensitivity, its life-cycle stage and the possible consequences.

scenes.heading: See it early
scenes.narration: The bank needs robust mechanisms to detect and respond to incidents in a timely way. Prevention alone is never enough.

scenes.heading: Plans for the plausible
scenes.narration: It must keep response plans for incidents that could plausibly happen, covering every stage from detection to post-incident review, plus escalation to the board.

scenes.heading: Test and test again
scenes.narration: Response plans must be reviewed and tested every year. Controls must be tested through a systematic program run by skilled, functionally independent specialists.

scenes.heading: Independent eyes
scenes.narration: Internal audit must review the design and operating effectiveness of security controls, including controls run by third parties.

scenes.heading: Tell the regulator
scenes.narration: Material incidents go to APRA within 72 hours of becoming aware. Material control weaknesses that won't be fixed in time go to APRA within 10 business days.

cards.title: The CPS 234 incident cycle
cards.caption: Response plans must cover every stage from detection to post-incident review.

items.label: Detect
items.detail: Monitoring and staff reports surface an actual or potential compromise.

items.label: Assess and escalate
items.detail: Rate materiality; escalate to the board and responsible owners as the plan sets out.

items.label: Contain and respond
items.detail: Follow the tested response plan; preserve evidence.

items.label: Notify
items.detail: APRA within 72 hours if material or notified to other regulators; other regimes as they apply.

items.label: Review and improve
items.detail: Post-incident review feeds controls, testing and training.

cards.title: Two APRA notification clocks in CPS 234
cards.caption: Both deadlines come from CPS 234. 'As soon as possible' comes first; the outer limit is a backstop.

items.label: What triggers it
items.left: Incident that materially affected, or could have, the bank or customers; or was notified to another regulator
items.right: Material control weakness the bank expects it cannot fix in a timely way

items.label: Deadline
items.left: As soon as possible, no later than 72 hours
items.right: As soon as possible, no later than 10 business days

items.label: Clock starts
items.left: When the bank becomes aware of the incident
items.right: When the bank becomes aware of the weakness

items.label: Typical example
items.right: Privileged accounts lack strong authentication, and the fix is months away

cards.question: A bank discovers a material information security incident on Monday at 10 am. What is the latest it may notify APRA under CPS 234?
options: Within 10 business days
Thursday at 10 am, 72 hours after becoming aware, and sooner if possible
Only after its forensic investigation is complete
At the next scheduled supervision meeting
cards.explanation: CPS 234 requires notice as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware. The 10-business-day limit applies to material control weaknesses, not incidents.

cards.title: Testing that means something
cards.body:
CPS 234 does not let a bank mark its own homework. Its testing rules are specific:

- A **systematic testing program** checks whether controls work. How often and how deeply each control is tested depends on how fast threats change, the asset's criticality and sensitivity, the consequences of an incident, exposure to untrusted environments, and how often the asset changes.
- Testers must be **appropriately skilled and functionally independent**.
- Deficiencies that **cannot be fixed in a timely way** are escalated to the board or senior management.
- The program itself is reviewed **at least annually**, or sooner after a material change.
- If a third party tests its own controls, the bank must judge whether that testing is deep and frequent enough.
- **Internal audit** gives separate assurance on design and operating effectiveness, using skilled people.

APRA's guide CPG 234 lists techniques such as penetration tests, social engineering tests and access reviews.

cards.title: Which CPS 234 clock applies?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the APRA notification it most likely triggers.
buckets: No APRA notice on these facts

items.text: Attackers encrypt the core banking servers and branches cannot serve customers
Bank reports a data theft to an overseas regulator where it has a branch
Audit finds no strong authentication on privileged admin access; fix needs a year-long rebuild
An unsupported system holding customer data cannot be patched for months
A phishing email is reported and deleted; no one clicked and no access occurred
A minor control gap is found and fixed the same week
Card data at an outsourced processor is accessed by an intruder

cards.title: The quiet weakness
cards.setting: Mei's office, Brisbane. Two weeks later.

lines.text: The penetration test is back. Our internet banking admin console still accepts a password alone for privileged staff.
Can we fix it this sprint?
Vendor says the platform needs an upgrade first. Realistic date: nine months away.
Nine months of exposure on the keys to the kingdom. What does the standard expect from us now?

cards.title: Nine months to fix the admin console
cards.situation: A penetration test shows privileged access to the internet banking admin console uses a password only. The vendor says a fix needs a platform upgrade about nine months away. The test was run by an independent firm. The head of digital wants to 'keep it in the team' until the upgrade lands.

choices.text: Accept the vendor date, log the finding and revisit after the upgrade.
choices.outcome: This ignores two CPS 234 duties: escalating deficiencies that cannot be fixed in time to the board or senior management, and notifying APRA of a material weakness the bank cannot fix in a timely way.

choices.text: Add compensating controls now, escalate to senior management and the board, assess materiality and, if material, notify APRA within 10 business days.
choices.outcome: This is the expected path. Compensating controls cut exposure, escalation meets the testing rules, and a material weakness that cannot be fixed in time is notified to APRA as soon as possible and within 10 business days.

choices.text: Ask the testing firm to remove the finding from the final report.
choices.outcome: Suppressing a finding defeats the purpose of independent testing and would hide a known weakness from the board and APRA. It could also mislead the regulator.

choices.text: Add compensating controls and fix it quietly within the digital team.
choices.outcome: Compensating controls help, but CPS 234 also requires escalation and, for a material weakness, notice to APRA. Keeping it in the team leaves the board blind.

cards.title: Run the response plan
cards.prompt: Put the first hours of a well-run incident response in order.
steps: Analyst confirms the alert is a real or potential compromise and opens an incident
Incident lead contains the threat, for example by blocking the address and isolating the server
Evidence such as logs and disk images is preserved for investigation
Materiality is assessed and the incident is escalated to executives and the board as the plan requires
APRA is notified as soon as possible and within 72 hours if the incident is material
A post-incident review records lessons and updates controls, tests and training

cards.question: Which of these does CPS 234 require for the testing of security controls?
options: Testing only by the vendor that built the system
Skilled and functionally independent testers, with the program reviewed at least annually
A fixed quarterly penetration test for every system, whatever its risk
cards.explanation: The standard requires skilled, functionally independent specialists and an annual (or change-driven) review of the program. Frequency and depth are risk-based rather than one fixed schedule.

cards.title: Real case: ASIC v FIIG Securities (2026)
Becoming aware is not the same as being certain
cards.body:
The 72-hour clock runs from when the bank **becomes aware** of the incident, and an incident includes a **potential** compromise. Don't wait for forensics to finish before telling the security office.

- Record the time you first saw the problem.
- Escalate through the plan's channel straight away.
- Share what you know, what you don't, and what you've done.
- Leave the materiality decision and the APRA notice to the incident lead and compliance.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Controls must be timely and sized to threats, criticality, sensitivity, life-cycle stage and consequences.
Response plans cover detection to post-incident review and must be reviewed and tested every year.
Testing is systematic, done by skilled and independent specialists, and the program is reviewed at least annually.
Notify APRA of a material incident within 72 hours of becoming aware, sooner if possible.
Notify APRA of a material control weakness that cannot be fixed in time within 10 business days.

cards.prompt: If you spotted something odd on a system tonight, who would you call, and how quickly could the bank's incident team know about it?

quiz.question: Under CPS 234, when must a bank notify APRA of a material information security incident?
options: As soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware
Within 30 days, once the investigation is complete
Within 24 hours of the incident starting
Within 10 business days of the board meeting
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 sets 72 hours from becoming aware, with 'as soon as possible' coming first. The 10-business-day limit is for material control weaknesses.

quiz.question: A bank tells a foreign regulator about a security incident affecting its overseas branch. The incident had little impact in Australia. Does CPS 234 require notice to APRA?
options: No: only incidents with a material impact on the bank or its Australian depositors count for APRA notice purposes
No: foreign incidents are reported in the annual return
Yes: an incident notified to other regulators, in Australia or overseas, must also be notified
Only if the foreign regulator asks APRA to be informed
quiz.explanation: One of the two triggers is that the incident has been notified to other regulators, domestic or international. Materiality in Australia is not required for that trigger.

quiz.question: How often must a bank review and test its information security response plans?
options: Every three years
Annually
Only after a material incident
Whenever APRA requests it
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 requires an annual review and test so that response plans remain effective and fit for purpose.

quiz.question: Internal testing shows a material control weakness that the bank expects to need eight months to fix. What does CPS 234 require?
options: Notify APRA within 72 hours, treating the weakness as an information security incident in its own right
Record it and report it only if it is exploited
Notify APRA only when the fix is complete
Notify APRA as soon as possible and within 10 business days of becoming aware
quiz.explanation: A material weakness the bank expects it cannot remediate in a timely way must be notified within 10 business days. The 72-hour rule is for incidents.

quiz.question: Which factor does CPS 234 NOT list for setting the nature and frequency of control testing?
options: The vendor's share price
How quickly vulnerabilities and threats change
The criticality and sensitivity of the asset
Exposure to environments where the bank cannot enforce its policies
quiz.explanation: The listed factors include rate of change of threats, criticality and sensitivity, consequences, untrusted environments and frequency of change. Commercial measures like share price are not among them.

quiz.question: Who may carry out the testing of security controls under CPS 234?
options: Any staff member who completed awareness training
Only APRA-accredited auditors
Appropriately skilled and functionally independent specialists
The team that designed and operates the control
quiz.explanation: Testers must be skilled and functionally independent. APRA does not accredit testers, and the team that runs a control lacks independence.

quiz.question: What must the response plans include under CPS 234?
options: A list of approved ransomware negotiators
Mechanisms for every incident stage and for escalation and reporting to the board and responsible people
A pre-written media release for each incident type, approved in advance by APRA's communications team
Only the contact details of the IT help desk
quiz.explanation: Plans must cover all stages from detection to post-incident review and the escalation and reporting of incidents to the board and others responsible for oversight.

quiz.question: What should happen to control deficiencies found in testing that cannot be fixed in a timely way?
options: They are closed once a risk owner signs an acceptance
They are deleted from the test report
They are fixed by the testers directly
They are escalated and reported to the board or senior management
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 requires escalation of such deficiencies to the board or senior management, and material ones may also trigger APRA notice.

quiz.question: In the FIIG Securities case, which failure did ASIC list?
options: No incident response plan tested at least annually
Using a cloud provider based overseas
Reporting the breach to clients too quickly
Encrypting data that clients did not ask to protect
quiz.explanation: ASIC listed missing MFA, patching, monitoring, testing, awareness training and an incident response plan tested at least annually. The other options were not failures in the case.

quiz.question: A night analyst sees a possible data exfiltration but is not sure it is real. What best supports CPS 234 compliance?
options: Wait until the morning team confirms it, because only a confirmed compromise counts as an incident for APRA
Notify APRA personally before telling anyone
Delete the alert if the data flow has stopped
Escalate now through the response plan; a potential compromise is already an incident
quiz.explanation: An incident includes a potential compromise, and the 72-hour clock runs from awareness. Escalation through the plan lets the incident lead assess materiality and handle notices.

sessions.title: The human firewall: awareness, phishing and social engineering
sessions.summary: Use APRA's CPG 234 guidance to build security awareness that works: who to train, what to cover, how to test understanding, and how to spot and report phishing, vishing, tailgating and other social engineering.
objectives: Describe the awareness program CPG 234 presents as sound practice
Recognise common social engineering techniques used against bank staff
Respond correctly to suspicious calls, emails and requests
Explain why awareness results are reported to the board

cards.title: Stage three: the human firewall
cards.setting: Contact centre floor, Wattle Coast Bank, Perth. Thursday, 9:20 am.

lines.text: Three calls this morning from 'IT support' asking agents to read out the code from their authenticator app. One agent nearly did.
That's a classic. Attackers can't beat multi-factor authentication technically, so they try to beat the person holding the phone.
We did the annual e-learning. People clicked through it in eleven minutes.
APRA's guidance pictures more than a tick-box: training tracked, understanding tested at the start and periodically, and topics that match how people are really attacked.
And the board wants evidence it works. Not just completion rates.
Then let's build an awareness program people remember. Stage three: turning staff from the weakest link into the first alarm.

scenes.heading: Guidance, not a rulebook
scenes.narration: CPG 234 is APRA's practice guide to CPS 234. It explains what sound practice looks like; it uses words like 'could' and 'would typically' rather than imposing new rules.

scenes.heading: Everyone with access
scenes.narration: It suggests a training and awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, plus material that helps the board and other governing bodies carry out their duties.

scenes.heading: Track and test
scenes.narration: Sound practice tracks who completed training and tests whether people understand the security policies, both when they start and periodically after that.

scenes.heading: Real attack techniques
scenes.narration: Topics typically include email and internet use, malware, mobile devices, remote working, passwords and access, handling sensitive data, and common attacks on people such as social engineering and tailgating.

scenes.heading: Sign and report
scenes.narration: Users would typically sign off on security policies periodically as part of their terms, and everyone should know how to report incidents and concerns.

cards.title: A CPG 234-style awareness program
cards.caption: Built from the topics and practices in CPG 234 Attachment B and the board reporting examples in Attachment H.

items.label: Induction
items.detail: Security policies, reporting channels and a short understanding test before system access.

items.label: Role-based modules
items.detail: Deeper content for contact centre, payments, privileged IT users and executives.

items.label: Ongoing campaigns
items.detail: Phishing simulations, short refreshers and alerts on current scams.

items.label: Policy sign-off
items.detail: Periodic acknowledgement of security policies under employment or contract terms.

items.label: Measure and report
items.detail: Coverage, test scores and phishing results reported to management and the board.

cards.question: How does APRA's CPG 234 relate to the binding standard CPS 234?
options: It replaces CPS 234 for smaller banks
It is guidance on how to meet CPS 234, describing sound practice such as awareness training
It is a law passed by Parliament
It only applies to superannuation trustees
cards.explanation: CPG 234 is a prudential practice guide that supports CPS 234 for all APRA-regulated industries. It describes sound practice; CPS 234 holds the binding requirements.

cards.title: How a social engineering attack narrows in
cards.caption: Every stage is a chance to spot the attack. The ask is the last and clearest warning sign.

items.label: Research
items.detail: Attacker gathers names, roles and jargon from public profiles and past leaks.

items.label: Pretext
items.detail: A believable story: IT support, a senior executive, a regulator, a supplier.

items.label: Contact
items.detail: Email, text, phone call, collaboration chat or a visitor at the door.

items.label: Pressure
items.detail: Urgency, authority or fear to stop the target from checking.

items.label: The ask
items.detail: A code, a password, a payment change or a click.

items.text: Caller from 'IT' asks you to read out your authenticator code
Email from the CEO's personal address asks for an urgent supplier payment
A visitor without a pass follows you through the secure door holding coffee
Text says your bank login expires today and links to a look-alike page
Customer passes the bank's standard identification steps and asks for a balance
Help desk ticket you raised is closed through the official service portal
A 'supplier' calls to change bank account details and wants it done before lunch
Security team sends a scheduled reminder through the usual intranet channel

cards.title: Why phishing results reach the board
cards.body:
CPG 234 gives examples of security information a board could receive. Among them are **awareness exercise coverage** and the **share of staff responding to phishing tests**.

That matters for three reasons:

- **Board responsibility.** Under CPS 234 the board is ultimately responsible. It cannot judge whether the human layer is working from completion rates alone.
- **Testing applies to people too.** CPG 234 lists **social engineering tests** as a way to check access controls and staff awareness.
- **Trends beat snapshots.** Click rates, report rates and time-to-report, tracked over months, show whether training changes behaviour.

A good simulation program is **fair**: no humiliation, quick coaching after a click, and praise for fast reporting. The goal is a culture where reporting feels normal, because staff who report quickly turn one person's mistake into an early warning.

cards.title: The 'urgent' call
cards.setting: Contact centre floor, Perth. Friday, 4:47 pm.

lines.text: Agent Tayla waves Raj over and mutes her headset.
What's happening?
Tayla says the caller claims to be from the bank's cyber team. He says her account is part of an active breach and needs her authenticator code within two minutes to 'lock it'.
He knows her name, her manager's name and our ticket system's name. It sounds real.

cards.title: Two minutes to lock the account
cards.situation: A caller claiming to be from the bank's cyber team tells a contact centre agent that her account is compromised. He knows her name, her manager and internal system names, and asks for her authenticator code within two minutes to 'lock' the account. It is late on Friday. You are the team leader.

choices.text: Tell the agent to give the code, since the caller knows internal details and time is short.
choices.outcome: Internal details are easy to gather and are exactly what a pretext relies on. Real security teams never need your one-time code. The attacker now has a working session.

choices.text: Tell the agent to end the call, report it through the security channel at once, and call the security team back on the number in the bank directory.
choices.outcome: Correct. Verifying through a known channel defeats the pretext, and fast reporting lets security warn other agents and check for related attempts. This is the behaviour CPG 234-style training aims for.

choices.text: Tell the agent to hang up and forget about it, since nothing was disclosed.
choices.outcome: Hanging up is right, but not reporting wastes the early warning. The same caller is probably trying other agents right now.

cards.back: Fraudulent emails that push you to click, open an attachment or enter credentials on a fake page.
Voice phishing: a phone call using a pretext such as IT support, a regulator or a customer to extract information.
Phishing by text message, often with a link to a look-alike login page.
Following an authorised person through a secure door without using a pass.
Flooding someone with login approval prompts until they approve one just to make them stop.
Trying usernames and passwords leaked elsewhere against another service, hoping people reused them.
Using a hijacked or look-alike email account to redirect payments or obtain data.

cards.question: A staff member clicks a link in a simulated phishing email. What response best fits a healthy awareness culture?
options: Public naming in the weekly team meeting
Immediate dismissal
Short, private coaching, and encouragement to report quickly next time
Ignoring it because it was only a test
cards.explanation: The aim is behaviour change and fast reporting. Shaming discourages reporting; ignoring the result wastes the lesson. Coaching plus tracked trends gives the board meaningful evidence.

cards.title: Real case: APRA's 2025 letter on authentication controls
Real case: RI Advice and the brute force attack
Stage three take-aways
items: CPG 234 is APRA guidance; it describes an awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties.
Sound practice tracks training and tests understanding at commencement and periodically.
Typical topics include phishing, social engineering, tailgating, passwords, mobile and remote work, and reporting.
Never share a one-time code; verify any unexpected request through a channel you already know.
Phishing test results and awareness coverage are examples of what a board could receive.

cards.prompt: Which pretext would most likely fool you or your team: IT support, a senior executive, a supplier or a regulator? What one check would stop it?

quiz.question: What is CPG 234?
options: APRA's practice guide explaining sound practice for meeting CPS 234
A section of the Privacy Act 1988
An ASIC regulatory guide for financial advisers
A binding standard that replaced CPS 234 for banks when CPS 230 took effect in 2025
quiz.explanation: CPG 234 is APRA's prudential practice guide supporting CPS 234. It does not replace it and is not part of the Privacy Act or ASIC's guidance.

quiz.question: According to CPG 234, who would typically receive information security awareness training?
options: Only permanent staff in technology roles, because other staff are covered by the bank's code of conduct
Only customers using internet banking
Only staff who handle card data
Staff, contractors and third parties, with material for the board and governing bodies
quiz.explanation: CPG 234 describes communicating security expectations to staff, contractors and third parties, and providing material to help the board and other governing bodies carry out their duties.

quiz.question: When does CPG 234 describe testing staff understanding of security policies as sound practice?
options: Only after a security incident
On commencement and periodically after that
Only every five years
Only when staff change roles
quiz.explanation: The guide describes tracking training and testing understanding both on commencement and periodically.

quiz.question: A caller claiming to be from the bank's IT team asks an agent for the code shown in her authenticator app. What is the best response?
options: Give the code if the caller can correctly name the agent's manager and the internal ticketing system
Give only half of the code to test the caller
Refuse, end the call and report it, then verify through a known internal number
Ask the caller to email the request first, then comply
quiz.explanation: Legitimate teams never need a one-time code. A request by email can also be spoofed. Refusing, reporting and verifying through a known channel defeats the pretext.

quiz.question: Which attack relies on people reusing passwords leaked from another service?
options: Credential stuffing
Tailgating
MFA fatigue
Vishing
quiz.explanation: Credential stuffing tries leaked username and password pairs against other services. APRA's 2025 letter to superannuation trustees followed such attacks.

quiz.question: In its June 2025 letter after credential stuffing attacks, what did APRA say it expected at a minimum?
options: Passwords changed every thirty days for all members, with security questions added at every login
All online services to be closed until audited
Security questions instead of passwords for members
MFA or equivalent for high-risk activities and for all administrative or privileged access
quiz.explanation: APRA expected MFA or equivalent controls for high-risk activities and all administrative or privileged access, and required a self-assessment and, where deficient, a material control weakness notification or a rationale.

quiz.question: Which metric does CPG 234 give as an example of information a board could receive about the human layer of security?
options: The number of emails each employee sends
The share of staff responding to phishing tests
Staff satisfaction scores for the e-learning platform and its course catalogue
The cost of each e-learning licence
quiz.explanation: Attachment H of CPG 234 lists examples such as awareness exercise coverage and the percentage of staff responding to phishing tests.

quiz.question: A visitor without a pass follows an employee through a secure door. What is this called, and what should the employee do?
options: Smishing; report it to the privacy officer
Vishing; let them through if they look busy and appear to know the names of people on the floor
Tailgating; politely stop the person and direct them to reception or security
Credential stuffing; change their own password
quiz.explanation: Tailgating is following someone through a controlled entry. CPG 234 lists it among common attack techniques; the employee should not allow entry and should involve security.

quiz.question: Why is quick reporting of a phishing email valuable even if you did not click?
options: It automatically creates an APRA incident notification that must be lodged within 72 hours
Security can block the sender and warn others before someone else falls for it
It counts towards the employee's annual bonus
It removes the need for email filtering
quiz.explanation: Early reports let the security team act across the bank. Not every phishing email is an APRA-notifiable incident.

quiz.question: An executive gets an email from what looks like the chief executive's personal address asking for an urgent supplier payment. Which attack type is most likely?
options: Tailgating
Credential stuffing
MFA fatigue
Business email compromise
quiz.explanation: A spoofed or hijacked email used to redirect a payment is business email compromise. The fix is to verify through a known channel before paying.

sessions.title: Privacy Act 1988: APP 11 security and the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme
sessions.summary: Apply APP 11's duty to protect and dispose of personal information, then walk through Part IIIC: what an eligible data breach is, how to judge serious harm, the 30-day assessment and notice to the Commissioner and customers.
objectives: Explain the duties in APP 11.1, 11.2 and 11.3
Decide whether an incident is an eligible data breach, including remedial action
Describe the assessment and notification steps in Part IIIC
Coordinate Privacy Act and CPS 234 duties for the same incident

cards.title: Stage four: the privacy vault
cards.setting: Privacy office, Wattle Coast Bank, Brisbane. Tuesday, 10:00 am.

lines.text: A branch officer emailed a spreadsheet of 2,300 home loan customers, with incomes and tax file numbers, to the wrong external address.
Is that a cyber incident? Nobody hacked anything.
Under the Privacy Act it doesn't matter how it happened. It's an unauthorised disclosure of personal information. The question is whether serious harm is likely.
And from the CPS 234 side, it's a compromise of confidentiality. We assess materiality for APRA in parallel.
The recipient hasn't replied yet. If we get the file deleted fast, that changes the analysis. Let's walk through it properly.

cards.title: Privacy Act 1988: APP 11 and the NDB scheme

scenes.heading: The law
scenes.narration: The Privacy Act 1988 contains the Australian Privacy Principles. Banks, as organisations covered by the Act, must follow them. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, the OAIC, regulates it.

scenes.heading: APP 11.1
scenes.narration: If you hold personal information, you must take reasonable steps to protect it from misuse, interference and loss, and from unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.

scenes.heading: APP 11.2
scenes.narration: When you no longer need it for a permitted purpose, and no law or court order requires you to keep it, you must take reasonable steps to destroy or de-identify it.

scenes.heading: APP 11.3
scenes.narration: The Act now makes clear that reasonable steps include technical and organisational measures. Training staff is a classic organisational measure.

scenes.heading: Part IIIC
scenes.narration: Part IIIC of the Act sets up the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: eligible data breaches must be notified to the Commissioner and to affected individuals.

cards.title: Is it an eligible data breach?
cards.caption: Based on sections 26WE and 26WF of the Privacy Act 1988 (Part IIIC).

items.label: Personal information held
items.detail: The bank holds personal information it must protect under APP 11.

items.label: Unauthorised access, disclosure or loss
items.detail: Someone got it, it was sent out, or it was lost where that could happen.

items.label: Serious harm likely?
items.detail: Would a reasonable person conclude serious harm is likely for any individual?

items.label: Remedial action?
items.detail: If quick action means serious harm is no longer likely, it is not an eligible breach.

items.label: Eligible data breach
items.detail: Notify the Commissioner and affected individuals as soon as practicable.

cards.question: Which situation can be an eligible data breach under the Privacy Act?
options: Only a breach caused by an external hacker
Unauthorised access, disclosure or loss of personal information where serious harm is likely
Any system outage that delays payments
A customer complaint about marketing emails
cards.explanation: Part IIIC turns on unauthorised access, disclosure or loss of personal information that is likely to result in serious harm. Human error counts just as much as hacking.

cards.title: From suspicion to notification
cards.caption: Sections 26WH, 26WK and 26WL. The 30 days is an outer limit for the assessment, not a target.

items.label: Suspicion
items.detail: Reasonable grounds to suspect a breach: start a reasonable, fast assessment.

items.label: Assessment
items.detail: Take all reasonable steps to finish the assessment within 30 days of becoming aware.

items.label: Belief
items.detail: Reasonable grounds to believe: prepare a statement and give it to the Commissioner.

items.label: Individuals told
items.detail: Notify all affected or all at-risk individuals; if neither is practicable, publish and publicise.

cards.title: Judging 'serious harm'
cards.body:
The Act lists matters to weigh when deciding whether a reasonable person would conclude serious harm is likely (section 26WG). In your own assessment, ask:

- **What kind of information** is it, and how **sensitive**? Tax file numbers, identity documents, account details and health data weigh heavily.
- Was it **protected** by security measures, such as strong encryption, and how likely is it that someone could get around them (for example, was the key also exposed)?
- **Who** has, or could get, the information? A trusted bank partner is different from a criminal forum.
- What is the **nature of the harm**? Think identity theft, financial loss, threats to safety, humiliation or damage to reputation.
- Any **other relevant matters**.

**Remedial action counts.** If the bank acts before harm occurs and, as a result, a reasonable person would conclude serious harm is no longer likely, the breach is treated as never having been eligible (section 26WF). That is why fast reporting by staff matters so much.

cards.title: Who, what, when?
cards.prompt: Match each step of the NDB scheme to what it involves.

pairs.right: Run a reasonable and fast assessment, using all reasonable steps to finish within 30 days
Identity and contact details, a description of the breach, the kinds of information, recommended steps
All affected individuals, or all at risk; otherwise publish the statement and publicise it
Fast action that means serious harm is no longer likely, so no notification is needed
Information the bank sent overseas under APP 8 can still count as held by the bank for the scheme

cards.title: The reply from the wrong inbox

lines.text: The wrong recipient is a small accounting firm. They've confirmed in writing that they deleted the email and the file, and didn't open the attachment.
So we're done?
Not quite. We document the assessment, check their deletion confirmation is credible, and decide whether serious harm is still likely. And we fix why it happened.
A different case would play out very differently. Imagine the same file on a criminal forum.

cards.title: The leaked file on a forum
cards.situation: Monitoring finds that a file with names, dates of birth, driver licence numbers and account numbers of 9,000 Wattle Coast customers has been posted on a criminal forum. It came from a marketing supplier the bank shared data with. The supplier says it is 'still investigating' and asks the bank to say nothing for a month.

choices.text: Agree to wait a month so the supplier can complete its investigation.
choices.outcome: The bank already has reasonable grounds to believe an eligible breach has happened: sensitive identity data is in criminal hands. Waiting a month would breach the 'as soon as practicable' duty and leave customers unprotected.

choices.text: Treat it as an eligible data breach: prepare the statement for the Commissioner, notify affected customers with practical steps, assess CPS 234 materiality for APRA, and manage the supplier.
choices.outcome: Correct. Serious harm is likely, remedial action cannot pull the data back, and both regimes apply. Customers get advice such as replacing licences and watching accounts; APRA is told within 72 hours if material.

choices.text: Notify the Commissioner but not customers, to avoid panic.
choices.outcome: The Act requires notifying the contents of the statement to individuals (or publishing it if that is not practicable). Customers need to know so they can protect themselves.

cards.title: Eligible breach or not (on these facts)?
cards.prompt: Decide which outcome is more likely on the facts given.

items.text: Unencrypted laptop with customer tax file numbers stolen from a car
Encrypted backup tape lost; key stored separately and not exposed
Statement sent to wrong customer, who confirms deletion unopened within an hour
Attacker downloads identity documents from a cloud bucket left public
Customer database listed for sale on a criminal forum
Staff member views a colleague's account out of curiosity; no further disclosure and access is cut off fast

cards.question: Under section 26WH, how long does a bank have to complete its assessment of a suspected eligible data breach?
options: 72 hours
It must take all reasonable steps to complete it within 30 days
10 business days
There is no time limit
cards.explanation: The assessment must be reasonable and expeditious, and the entity must take all reasonable steps to complete it within 30 days of becoming aware of the grounds for suspicion. 72 hours is the CPS 234 APRA clock.

cards.front: Who regulates APP 11 and the NDB scheme?
cards.back: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).
APRA, within 72 hours of the bank becoming aware of a material incident.

cards.front: Does notifying the OAIC affect the CPS 234 duty?
cards.back: Yes. An incident notified to another regulator is one of the triggers for notifying APRA.

cards.front: Does a breach need a hacker?
cards.back: No. Misdirected emails, lost files and staff snooping can all be breaches.

cards.front: What should a staff member do first?
cards.back: Report the suspected breach immediately through the bank's channel, so assessment and remedial action can start.

cards.title: Real case: FIIG Securities notifies 18,000 clients
Stage four take-aways
items: APP 11.1 requires reasonable steps, including technical and organisational measures, to protect personal information.
APP 11.2 requires destroying or de-identifying information no longer needed, unless the law requires keeping it.
An eligible data breach is unauthorised access, disclosure or loss that is likely to cause serious harm.
Suspected breaches need a fast assessment, with all reasonable steps to finish within 30 days.
Eligible breaches go to the Commissioner and affected individuals as soon as practicable; consider APRA's 72-hour rule too.

cards.prompt: Where in your daily work could personal information be sent, left or shown to the wrong person? What habit would prevent it?

quiz.question: What does APP 11.1 of the Privacy Act 1988 require of a bank that holds personal information?
options: Encryption of all data using an algorithm approved by APRA
Storage of all personal information only within Australia, on systems inspected and certified each year by the OAIC
Reasonable steps to protect it from misuse, interference, loss and unauthorised access, modification or disclosure
Deletion of all customer data after seven years
quiz.explanation: APP 11.1 sets a reasonable-steps duty to protect against misuse, interference, loss and unauthorised access, modification or disclosure. It does not prescribe a specific algorithm, location or retention period.

quiz.question: What does APP 11.3 clarify about the 'reasonable steps' in APP 11?
options: They are limited to physical locks and alarms
They include technical and organisational measures
They are set out in a fixed list of controls made by APRA under CPS 234
They apply only to sensitive information
quiz.explanation: APP 11.3 states that reasonable steps include technical and organisational measures. Staff training and access controls are typical examples.

quiz.question: A bank no longer needs a former applicant's documents for any permitted purpose, and no law or court order requires it to keep them. What does APP 11.2 require?
options: Reasonable steps to destroy or de-identify the information
Keeping it indefinitely in case the person reapplies, provided it is stored securely
Sending it back to the person by registered post
Transferring it to the OAIC for archiving
quiz.explanation: APP 11.2 requires reasonable steps to destroy or de-identify personal information no longer needed, subject to legal retention duties.

quiz.question: An employee emails a customer list to the wrong external address. Which statement is correct under Part IIIC?
options: It cannot be a breach because it was an honest mistake
It is only a breach if the recipient is overseas
It is automatically notifiable to the Commissioner and every affected customer, regardless of the likelihood of harm
It can be an eligible data breach if serious harm is likely, even though no one hacked anything
quiz.explanation: Unauthorised disclosure through human error is covered. Whether it is eligible depends on whether a reasonable person would conclude serious harm is likely, after any remedial action.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a matter section 26WG lists for judging whether serious harm is likely?
options: The bank's share price after the breach
The sensitivity of the information
Whether security measures protected it and could be overcome
Who has obtained or could obtain the information
quiz.explanation: Section 26WG lists the kinds and sensitivity of information, security measures and their likelihood of being overcome, the persons who may obtain it, the nature of the harm and other relevant matters. Share price is irrelevant.

quiz.question: A lost backup tape is strongly encrypted and the key was stored separately and not exposed. How does this affect the serious harm assessment?
options: It reduces the likelihood of serious harm, because the security measure is unlikely to be overcome
It has no effect, because every loss of a device or tape holding personal information is notifiable regardless of protection
It makes the breach notifiable to APRA only
It means the Privacy Act does not apply to the tape
quiz.explanation: Section 26WG asks whether security measures protected the data and how likely they are to be overcome, noting an encryption key as information needed to get around encryption.

quiz.question: A bank suspects, but is not yet sure, that an eligible data breach has occurred. What must it do?
options: Notify all customers immediately to be safe
Wait until the breach is confirmed by police
Carry out a reasonable and fast assessment, taking all reasonable steps to finish within 30 days
Notify the Commissioner within 72 hours and all customers within 30 days, even before the assessment is finished
quiz.explanation: Section 26WH requires a reasonable and expeditious assessment, with all reasonable steps taken to complete it within 30 days. Notification follows once there are reasonable grounds to believe.

quiz.question: What must the statement to the Commissioner set out under section 26WK?
options: The names of the staff responsible for the breach and the disciplinary action the bank has taken against them
Identity and contact details, a breach description, kinds of information and recommended steps for individuals
An estimate of the bank's financial loss
The bank's proposed compensation offer
quiz.explanation: Section 26WK lists the entity's identity and contact details, a description of the breach, the kinds of information concerned and recommendations about steps individuals should take.

quiz.question: It is not practicable to contact affected customers or the at-risk group individually. What does section 26WL require instead?
options: Nothing further once the Commissioner is told
Ask APRA to contact the customers
Wait until up-to-date contact details can be found for every affected customer, however long that takes
Publish the statement on the bank's website and take reasonable steps to publicise it
quiz.explanation: Where neither individual notification option is practicable, the entity must publish the statement on its website (if any) and take reasonable steps to publicise its contents.

quiz.question: A bank notifies the OAIC of an eligible data breach caused by a cyber-attack. Why must it also consider CPS 234?
options: The OAIC forwards every notice to APRA automatically
CPS 234 replaces Part IIIC for APRA-regulated banks, so the OAIC notice was not actually required
An incident notified to another regulator triggers APRA notice within 72 hours
APRA must approve the statement before it is sent
quiz.explanation: CPS 234 requires notice to APRA for an incident notified to other regulators, as well as for material incidents. Neither regime replaces the other.

sessions.title: CPS 230 resilience, service providers and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: Learn CPS 230: critical operations, tolerance levels, the BCP and its testing, material service providers and APRA notices. Then pull everything together with board accountability and the evidence an audit expects.
objectives: Identify critical operations and the three dimensions of tolerance levels
Describe the BCP contents and testing duties under CPS 230
Apply CPS 230's material service provider requirements and notices
Summarise board accountability and the evidence a bank needs for review

cards.title: Stage five: the unbroken line
cards.setting: Crisis room, Wattle Coast Bank, Brisbane. Saturday, 7:10 am.

lines.text: A failed update at the bank's core technology provider has knocked out card payments and internet banking across the country.
Payments down for 90 minutes so far. Our board-approved tolerance for payments is four hours. Customer calls are tripling.
(from Perth) The queue is at 600. People can't buy groceries. We need a script, now.
This is exactly what CPS 230 asks of us: keep critical operations within tolerance through a severe disruption. Where's the BCP?
And we check it isn't also a security incident. A failed update and an attack can look the same in the first hour.
BCP activated at 6:55. Let's show the board the plan works. Final stage: resilience, and everything you need for the exam.

scenes.heading: New since 2025
scenes.narration: APRA's CPS 230 took effect on 1 July 2025, replacing the older standards on outsourcing and business continuity. A version with targeted amendments has applied since 1 July 2026.

scenes.heading: Full range of risks
scenes.narration: Banks must manage all their operational risks, including legal, compliance, conduct, technology, data and change management risk, and meet CPS 234 for information security.

scenes.heading: Critical operations
scenes.narration: A bank keeps a register of critical operations. For a deposit-taker, payments, deposit-taking and management, custody, settlements and clearing, and customer enquiries are critical unless it can justify otherwise.

scenes.heading: Tolerance levels
scenes.narration: For each critical operation the bank sets how long a disruption it would tolerate, how much data loss it would accept, and the minimum service it would keep running.

scenes.heading: Service providers
scenes.narration: Banks manage material service providers through a policy, a register, due diligence, formal agreements and monitoring, including risks from fourth parties.

scenes.heading: Board accountable
scenes.narration: The board is ultimately accountable for oversight of operational risk. It approves the business continuity plan and tolerance levels, and the service provider policy.

cards.title: Reading a disruption against tolerance
cards.caption: A teaching grid for the duties in CPS 230; your bank's BCP sets the actual triggers.

items.label: Inside tolerance, contained
items.detail: Run the BCP, monitor, communicate with customers.

items.label: Inside tolerance, worsening
items.detail: Prepare escalation; brief executives; ready APRA notice if it may breach.

items.label: Minor operation, short outage
items.detail: Normal incident management; record and learn.

items.label: Outside tolerance
items.detail: Notify APRA within 24 hours; report to the board with a remediation plan.

cards.question: Under CPS 230, which set must a bank define for each critical operation?
options: A marketing plan, a budget and a headcount
Maximum disruption time, maximum data loss and minimum service levels
A list of competitors offering the same service
cards.explanation: Tolerance levels cover the maximum tolerable disruption period, the maximum acceptable data loss and minimum service levels while operating under alternative arrangements.

cards.title: APRA notification clocks across CPS 234 and CPS 230
cards.caption: Every clock says 'as soon as possible' first. A CPS 234 notice need not be repeated under CPS 230's incident rule.

items.label: Material security control weakness (CPS 234)
items.right: Bank expects it cannot remediate in time

items.label: Material operational risk incident (CPS 230)
items.right: Likely material financial impact or threat to critical operations

items.label: New or changed arrangement for a critical operation (CPS 230)
items.right: After entering into or materially changing it

cards.title: The business continuity plan, unpacked
Material service providers
cards.prompt: Match each CPS 230 duty to what it means in practice.

pairs.right: Keep a register of material service providers and submit it to APRA every year
Credit assessment, funding and liquidity management, and mortgage brokerage providers
Risk management, core technology services and internal audit providers
Due diligence and an assessment of financial and non-financial risks, including concentration
Service levels, data ownership, audit access, APRA access, sub-contracting notice, termination
Tell APRA before entering a material arrangement where the service is performed outside Australia

cards.title: The board's question
cards.setting: Board risk committee, Brisbane. Monday, 9:00 am.

lines.text: Payments came back in two hours and forty minutes. Inside tolerance. Well done. But I have a question for the room.
The provider's failed update came from one of its own sub-contractors. Did we know that sub-contractor existed?
Not until Saturday.
Then our fourth-party view has a gap. CPS 230 wants our policy to cover fourth parties that material providers rely on for critical operations.
As directors we're accountable for oversight of this. What do we do next?

cards.title: Fixing the fourth-party blind spot
cards.situation: After a disruption caused by a sub-contractor of the bank's core technology provider, the board learns the bank had no record of that sub-contractor. Payments stayed within tolerance this time. Management proposes three options.

choices.text: Close the matter: tolerance was met, so there is no breach and no action needed.
choices.outcome: Meeting tolerance once does not show the arrangement is well managed. CPS 230 expects the policy to address fourth-party risk and the contract to require notice of material sub-contracting.

choices.text: Update the service provider policy and register for fourth parties, require sub-contracting notice in the contract, include provider failure in the next BCP exercise and report progress to the board.
choices.outcome: This addresses the root cause and matches CPS 230: fourth-party risk in the policy, contract terms on sub-contracting, severe but plausible scenarios including provider failure, and board oversight.

choices.text: Replace the provider immediately with the cheapest alternative.
choices.outcome: An unplanned exit adds risk. CPS 230 expects due diligence before entering a new material arrangement and an orderly exit plan, not a rushed switch.

choices.text: Ask the provider for a list of sub-contractors, file it, and take no other action.
choices.outcome: A list is a start, but without policy, contract terms, testing and monitoring, the blind spot will come back.

cards.title: Readiness: the bank's year of assurance
cards.prompt: Order these steps of a well-run security and resilience year, starting from setting direction.
steps: Board approves risk appetite, tolerance levels, the BCP and the service provider policy
Management classifies information assets and maps the resources behind each critical operation
Controls are implemented and staff complete induction and periodic awareness training
Independent specialists test controls, and the response plan and BCP are exercised
Internal audit reviews control effectiveness and the credibility of the BCP
Results, weaknesses and remediation plans are reported to the board, and APRA is notified where required

cards.back: As soon as possible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a material incident or one notified to other regulators.
As soon as possible, no later than 10 business days for a material weakness the bank cannot fix in time.
As soon as possible, no later than 24 hours after a disruption to a critical operation outside tolerance.
Reasonable and fast, with all reasonable steps to finish within 30 days.
Test the security response plan; review the testing program; run a BC exercise; update the BCP; submit the material service provider register.
The board: for information security (CPS 234) and oversight of operational risk (CPS 230).

cards.question: Which business operations must a bank treat as critical under CPS 230 unless it can justify otherwise?
options: Marketing, branch design and sponsorship
Payments, deposit-taking and management, custody, settlements and clearing, and customer enquiries
Only the operations its board chooses each year
Only services provided by overseas providers
cards.explanation: CPS 230 lists these as minimum critical operations for a deposit-taking institution, together with customer enquiries and the systems and infrastructure that support critical operations.

cards.title: Real case: accountability after the Medibank incident
cards.body:
When APRA acted against **Medibank** in **June 2023**, it did not stop at controls. It said it expected **appropriate accountability and consequence management**, including impacts on **executive remuneration** where appropriate, and announced a technology review focused on **governance and risk culture**.

APRA also said it continued to see poor cyber practices and **inadequate oversight from boards and management** across regulated entities, and would act where needed.

**Why it matters for a bank's directors:**

- CPS 234 makes the board ultimately responsible for information security, and CPS 230 makes it ultimately accountable for oversight of operational risk.
- Boards need meaningful reporting: incidents, test results, control gaps, tolerance breaches and provider performance.
- APRA can impose capital adjustments, require reviews and expects consequences for executives when controls fail.

cards.title: Real case: what failure cost FIIG
cards.body:
When the Federal Court ordered **FIIG Securities** to pay **AUD 2.5 million** in **2026**, ASIC noted that the consequences were far larger than the cost of putting adequate controls in place at the start. Beyond the penalty and AUD 500,000 in costs, FIIG had to run a compliance program with an **independent expert** reviewing its cyber security and resilience systems.

Among the failures FIIG admitted: not allocating enough money for qualified people and technology, no MFA for remote access, no structured patching plan, no monitoring of threat alerts, **no mandatory cyber security awareness training** for staff, and no incident response plan tested at least annually.

**Readiness lesson:** every item on that list maps to something a bank's own program should show at audit: resourcing, controls, testing, training records and tested plans.

cards.title: Stage five take-aways
